newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: FEATURE - Work begins early for Kabul's children.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Work begins early for Kabul's children.

text.p: Abdul Memon is twelve years old. He works full time as an apprentice welder for the equivalent of 44 cents a week.

He works in a metal shop -- little more than an old shipping container with an awning over the front -- in Kabul's Karte Parwan market. He hammers, saws and bends metal sheets which are later made into doors.
In a recent survey, the non-governmental organisation Terre des Hommes estimated there are about 28,000 children working on the streets in the Afghan capital.

Seventeen years of war have destroyed the extended family network that used to provide a rudimentary safety net for Kabul's poorest residents. Family members have been killed or scattered as the tides of war washed over the city.
Successive administrations in Kabul have been tied up in the fighting and the social services that have survived have devolved to the few international organisations who still operate in Kabul.

For the last four years, before Kabul fell to the fighters of the Taleban movement in late September, the city was under siege. Food prices soared and aid workers said many people had to sell their belongings to survive.

Even after the seige, the situation remains critical. The United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) intends to increase food distribution from 2,500 tonnes a month to 3,500 tonnes a month, said Ismael Omer, head of WFP in Kabul.
The labour of their children has become a vital component of many family incomes.
Abdul Memon works eight hours a day, six days a week for his 44 cents.

He has started to learn how to weld, from someone only slightly older than himself, and proudly wears an old pair of plastic sunglasses hung round his neck by a piece of string. They are his only protection against the blinding light of the welding arc.
Memon says he has worked in the shop for two years, earning money to help his father support their family.
"I have two small brothers and a small sister. My father is a porter, but he does not earn enough," he said.
Memon says his ambition is to have his own shop. "I want to open my own metal working shop, but that it will take a long time to earn the money to buy the equipment and a place to work," he said.

Haroun is fourteen and has recently qualified as a welder. As an ancient generator made of a fume-belching Russian truck engine chugged in the background, he explained that his promotion has meant a rise in his salary.
"I used to earn 10,000 Afghanis (56 cents) a week, now I earn 15,000 Afghanis (83 cents)," said Haroun.

He said his father died seven years ago, and that he and his brother who works for the government between them support nine people. The sum of their salaries amounts to the equivalent of $2.30 per week.

Amrulla works a little way down the street from Memon and Haroun putting loose charcoal into sacks. He receives no money for his work, just seven kilos of charcoal per day. Terre des Hommes say 30 percent, or 8,400, of Kabul's working children work to provide their families with fuel.
Amrulla says his father sells onions when they are in season, but that it does not earn enough money to feed and keep warm the 10 people in his family.
The brutal Afghan winter will be on Kabul in earnest in another month, with temperatures dropping to minus 20 degrees C (-4 Fahrenheit) at night.
The contributions of Memon, Haroun, Amrulla and the thousands like them will become even more critical to the survival of their families.
